LIFT THE SURFACE

Follow what makes it work.

Choose a journey through the architecture.

From a visitor to a storefront.

REQUEST PATH
  1. 01 / EDGE
    Public HTTPS

    DNS and the edge path bring the visitor to the cluster’s ingress.

  2. 02 / ROUTING
    Traefik

    The hostname selects the storefront Service; cert-manager manages its TLS certificate.

  3. 03 / SERVING
    Next.js × 2

    Two configured replicas on separate workers serve the interface and server routes.

  4. 04 / COMMERCE
    Medusa

    Server-side integration connects commerce operations to the backend. Demo catalog mode supplies browsing examples.

The engineering decision: availability has boundaries

Required hostname anti-affinity separates storefront pods. A disruption budget and one-at-a-time rolling updates protect the serving tier when capacity is available. Backend data, storage, ingress, and the edge each have their own recovery requirements; two storefront pods do not make the entire system highly available.

From a source change to a new image.

DELIVERY DESIGN
  1. 01 / SOURCE
    GitHub Actions

    Checks and a standalone Next.js build precede image publication. Runner selection supports a hosted fallback.

  2. 02 / ARTIFACT
    GHCR

    Main-branch builds publish a production channel and a commit-specific tag for traceability.

  3. 03 / DESIRED STATE
    Argo CD

    Antalos owns Kubernetes configuration. Argo reconciles the application manifests from Git.

  4. 04 / REFRESH
    Digest → rollout

    A separate image-refresh controller detects a new channel digest and requests a rolling update.

The engineering decision: configuration and images have separate owners

Argo CD owns deployment configuration; the refresh controller changes only its designated pod-template annotation. Sealed Secrets hold Kubernetes credentials. Commit-specific image tags support rollback. A successful build, a published image, ready pods, and a working public transaction are separate verification steps.

A storefront connected to business tools.

INTEGRATION DESIGN
  1. 01 / IDENTITY
    Customer sign-in

    Google customer authentication connects through Medusa, with server-side credentials and cookie-bound callback state.

  2. 02 / SUPPORT
    Zammad

    The contact API creates support tickets. Redis guards rate limits and duplicate submissions.

  3. 03 / PROFILES
    Odoo + Mautic

    Customer-sync code connects commerce profiles to ERP contacts and marketing preferences.

  4. 04 / RESILIENCE
    Durable decisions

    Database-backed sync work supports retries and reconciliation. Consent and suppression rules govern marketing delivery.

The engineering decision: remote outages should not block signup

The customer-sync design queues delivery rather than calling Odoo or Mautic inside signup and checkout. Stable identifiers, retry backoff, and reconciliation handle remote failures; opt-outs take precedence. This describes the implementation design, without asserting that migrations, provisioning, or external flows have been verified in production.

FIELD NOTES / 001
configure→deploy→repeat
INFRASTRUCTURE, ONE STEP AT A TIME.

SELF-HOSTING · 1 MIN READ

A small start to repeatable deployments

One service, a clear configuration, and a little documentation go a long way.

Start small

A home lab does not need to begin with a dozen services. Pick one useful application, give it a home, and learn how it starts, stores data, and recovers after a restart.

Make it repeatable

Keep the configuration in Git and write down the deployment steps. The goal is simple: rebuilding the service should feel familiar instead of becoming a new investigation.

A working service is useful. A service you can rebuild is even better.

Leave a note

Record one thing that surprised you and one thing to improve next time. Those small notes become the most useful documentation in the lab.
